description: We’re Team HALO, a group of students from Riyadh who love space, games and building things that actually work. We split the work like a real mission crew: programmers built the game engine and the AI director, a teammate designed the four repair minigames, and the rest of us wrote the script, checked every science fact against NASA sources, and play-tested builds together. We wanted to make something a 9y/o would really want to play, that still teaches the hard choices real mission planners face
summary:
HALO is a free browser game where kids ages 7–12 command a four-person crew through 30 Martian days, managing resources to bring everyone home.

The first sol is fixed. After that, AI mission director A.R.C.H.E.R. generates daily crises shaped by past choices: clogged water recyclers, dusty solar panels, and repairs that fail again. Players pick three imperfect solutions: Fix (complete a hands-on oxygen, water, power, or shielding minigame), Borrow (use reserves and risk later costs), or Cut Back (save one resource by sacrificing another).

Each decision updates Power, Life Support, Shield, and Mission Progress with clear icons and numbers. Each sol ends with a simple “Why?” lesson explaining the science and consequences.

Real-world data powers the experience: NASA DONKI tracks recent solar storms that affect shield wear and crew radiation; Curiosity’s detector provides measurements from the May 2024 solar storm; NASA OSDR and RadLab inform lessons on sleep, bone loss, and radiation; Mars Trek maps actual landing sites; Microsoft Planetary Computer shows recent imagery of Houston Mission Control to explain Earth–Mars communication delays; and Meteomatics compares live Houston weather with Martian temperatures.

Every run changes with player decisions, encouraging experimentation and learning. Four possible endings lead to a debrief of lessons, defining choices, crew radiation dose, and all data sources used.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

HALO is an educational Mars outpost survival and mission-command simulation built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. Players take the role of the Commander leading a 4-person crew (Commander, Leila, Mateo, and Nia) alongside A.R.C.H.E.R., an onboard decision-support system, across a 30-Sol short stay or 50-Sol long stay on Mars, with an optional Hard Mode featuring a 14-Sol solar conjunction communication blackout.

Each Sol, the outpost faces system faults and environmental hazards across four core mission areas: Life Support, Power, Radiation Shield, and Mats for Launch. Players manage interdependent resources and crew radiation exposure, tracking cumulative dose in mSv against the 600 mSv NASA-STD-3001 career limit with a 0.65 mSv/sol baseline plus solar radiation storms. Players can use Ask Earth for Mission Control guidance, which arrives after a 3 to 22 minute one-way light-time delay scaled to an in-game countdown, or make an independent decision immediately. During Hard Mode's solar conjunction blackout, Earth help is unavailable. When systems fail, players complete hands-on engineering minigames including Water Recycler, Oxygen Filter, Food Production, Radiation Shield, and Circuit Repair, and review daily cause-and-effect reports grounded in NASA reference data such as Curiosity RAD storm readings, NASA DONKI solar activity, InSight dust/solar patterns, MOXIE oxygen production, and ISS ECLSS and OSDR research.

What benefits and intended impact does it have?

HALO turns abstract spaceflight constraints—life-support trade-offs, cumulative radiation risk, and Earth-Mars communication latency—into an interactive, hands-on experience. It helps students, aspiring engineers, and the general public understand why Martian astronauts must make autonomous decisions without real-time help from Earth and how every engineering shortcut creates downstream consequences.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, and software did you use?

We developed HALO using Unity 6 (6000.6.3f1) and C# (uGUI and TextMeshPro), built for WebGL on Unity Play and Windows. We used Blender for 3D outpost and character assets, ElevenLabs for pre-recorded and live-synthesized character voices (with browser text-to-speech fallback), and NASA DONKI, archived Curiosity RAD data, and Microsoft Planetary Computer / weather feeds for environmental context.

How is your project creative, and what factors did your team consider?

Instead of treating Mars survival as disconnected sliders or random disasters, HALO pairs a causal incident director—where quick fixes create future technical debt—with five distinct repair minigames and character-voiced briefings. Our team focused on player clarity by simplifying complex subsystem telemetry into four clear bars (Life Support, Power, Radiation Shield, and Mats for Launch) plus a dedicated Radiation (mSv) meter, while grounding the simulation in realistic Mars constraints like 3 to 22 minute signal delays, solar conjunction blackouts, 0.65 mSv/sol background radiation, and the 600 mSv limit as an approachable educational prototype.
